messages.author: 80ad59d3d3e3fe6f
messages.subject: AKDE or KDE more appropriate?
parts:
Hi, 

I just want to make sure I'm understanding this correctly and using the right home range analysis based on my data. I spot-mapped warbler territories once a week (for an hour at a time) over a 4 month breeding season and collected ~30-100 points per individual during the entire breeding season. I was running variograms in ctmm and they all look non range resident but I know they were because all the points were in the same area and each individual was on territory. I'm assuming the variograms look this way because of the low sample size and frequency at which I spot mapped these birds. I'm assuming this means fitting a movement model and running AKDEs on these birds would not be appropriate, a regular KDE would be better? 

Thanks, 

Michael

messages.author: 7d868ffe3daa8319
messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] AKDE or KDE more appropriate?
parts:
Hi Michael,

It's hard to say without seeing the variograms, but it is possible that even though the birds are staying in the same general area, they are gradually using larger amounts of space over time--e.g., because food is getting harder to find close to the nest so they have to cover more ground daily. If this is the case, the animal's movement pattern is not stationary, and no home range estimate is going to be informative. Performing conventional KDE will give you a number, but it won't be biologically or statistically meaningful.

If conventional KDE will provide the best estimate, the ctmm.select() function will choose the IID model. So you don't really ever need to worry about whether you should use KDE instead of AKDE--if you should, ctmm will automatically use KDE.

Jesse

messages.author: 7d868ffe3daa8319
messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] AKDE or KDE more appropriate?
parts:
Hi Michael,

This is a totally fine variogram, and pretty representative of the type of variogram we often see from VHF telemetry. The deviations from the asymptote are mostly random noise from small sample sizes at the individual time lags. What you really don't want to see is a line steadily going up, or a sweeping bell-shaped curve.

Jesse
